cl_lsd_chromosomes.short: Studies from 1967 to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes after pure LSD. Early reports of more breaks came mostly from people using many drugs.
cl_lsd_chromosomes.but: Small studies that only looked at blood cells under a microscope; the best had no group without LSD.
how: The 1967 scare began with LSD added to blood cells from two people in a lab dish, plus one patient with no 'before' test.
Two 1967 studies found more breaks in people who had taken LSD, with no 'before' test. In one, patients on other drugs but no LSD had about as many breaks.
The best study tested 32 patients before and after pure LSD. Damaged cells went from about 4 in 100 to 6, maybe by chance.
All these studies looked at blood cells under a microscope, not sperm or eggs. A 1971 review linked raised breaks mainly to street LSD and many other drugs.
cl_lsd_chromosomes.rate: Small, old studies of blood cells under a microscope. The best had no group without LSD, the studies disagree, and those that found more damage could not tell LSD apart from other drugs.

lsd.statement: Studies of people given pure LSD found clearly more broken chromosomes.
lsd.why: In studies from 1967 to 1970, microscope tests found no clear rise. Early reports of more breaks came mostly from people using many drugs.

lsd.statement: The early studies that linked LSD to broken chromosomes ruled out other drugs.
lsd.why: They did not. In one, patients on other drugs but no LSD had about as many breaks as people who had taken LSD.

lsd.q: Where did the 1967 LSD chromosome scare come from?
options: Cells from two people in a dish
Tests on thousands of people who used LSD
Babies born to mothers who took LSD
lsd.why: Cells from two people in a dish: LSD was added to their blood cells in a lab. Cells in a dish aren't people.
